state: The corn came straight off the grill, charred in spots, rolled in tangy crema and crumbled cotija, then dusted with chili powder and a hard squeeze of lime — the cob was the only plate anyone bothered with.

We grabbed a grilled ham and cheese from the market stand because the kids were starving, and the vendor spread the inside with a thin béchamel and dijon before pressing it flat — gone in five bites, worth the line.
Oh, you have to try this — chicken thighs braised low and slow in red wine with bacon lardons and pearl onions, finished with a knob of cold butter whisked in right at the end to glaze the sauce!

Sunday soup, ready in 20 minutes:
- well-fermented kimchi, roughly chopped
- soft tofu cubes
- gochugaru and a spoon of gochujang
- simmered in anchovy broth until the kimchi softens

Everything starts the night before, when I trim a shoulder of pork into thin sheets and drown them in a paste of dried guajillo and ancho chiles that have been toasted just until fragrant, soaked in hot water, then blended with a hit of pineapple juice, cider vinegar, garlic, cumin, and a spoon of achiote paste until the whole mixture turns the color of a sunset. The meat goes into the fridge overnight, and by morning it's stained a deep brick red clear through. I don't own a vertical spit, so I improvise by stacking the marinated slices onto skewers threaded through a coffee can propped over indirect coals, with a whole peeled onion wedged on top to catch the drippings and a few rings of fresh pineapple slid on near the end so they caramelize in the fat. When the outer layer has gone dark and crisp, I shave it off in thin curls straight onto a stack of small warm corn tortillas — always two, doubled up so they don't tear — and top everything with a scattering of diced white onion, a fistful of chopped cilantro, a few chunks of the charred pineapple, and a squeeze of lime. My neighbors know when I'm cooking this because the smell of toasted chiles drifts down the whole block by noon.

My uncle cook this stew every Sunday for many years, is big family recipe. First he toast dry guajillo chile and ancho chile and pasilla chile on hot pan, not too long or they get bitter. Then he put them in hot water for soften, and blend together with garlic, cumin seed, dry oregano, and two bay leaf. Goat meat or sometime beef, he braise it slow in this red sauce for almost four hours, until meat is falling from bone very easy. When is ready, he skim the orange fat from top and keep separate in small bowl. We dip corn tortilla straight into the hot fatty broth before we eat, this is best part, everybody fighting for it. Meat goes in small bowl with much broth, and on top we put chopped white onion, fresh cilantro, and squeeze of lime, sometimes little bit of raw chile too for who like spicy. My uncle say the secret is toasting chile properly, if you skip this step the stew taste flat and sad, no depth. We eat this with cold soda even on hot day, family tradition, nobody complain.

My grandmother fry small milk balls until they turn brown color, then soak them long time in sugar syrup with cardamom pods and few drops rose water, we eat them warm on festival night, very very sweet.

Fourteen dollars for onion soup, and somehow I don't even mind. The onions cook down for over an hour until they're jammy and almost black, drowned in beef stock and a splash of dry white wine, then the whole crock gets crowned with a toasted baguette slice and enough melted Gruyère to require a bib. Worth every cent, apparently.
Yesterday's fried tortilla chips get a second life drowning in salsa roja, crema, crumbled cotija, and a fried egg on top — breakfast, or an excuse to eat chips for breakfast, same thing really.

Okay so this week has been an absolute circus — Ben's soccer team made it to the semifinal (we lost, but the snacks were incredible, somebody's dad brought a whole watermelon carved like a turtle), and then the dishwasher decided to flood the kitchen on the exact same day the plumber was on vacation, so we've been hand-washing everything in the bathtub like it's 1950. Anyway, in between all that chaos I somehow still managed to get dinner on the table, which honestly felt like a small miracle. The fish had been sitting in the fridge marinating since the night before, just black cod fillets sitting in a mix of dashi, mirin, soy sauce, and a spoon of sugar, and I let it simmer gently on low heat until the glaze went thick and glossy and almost mahogany-colored, brushing it over the fillets every few minutes so it built up in layers. My neighbor Priya stopped by right as I was plating it and got roped into staying for dinner, which was fine because she brought a bottle of something sparkling and we ended up talking for two hours about her kitchen renovation, which is apparently three months behind schedule because the tile she wanted got discontinued. We also somehow got onto the topic of whether raccoons can open childproof latches (they can, we have photographic proof), and by the time she left it was nearly eleven and I still hadn't loaded the dishwasher that doesn't work. Tomorrow I'm supposed to bring cupcakes to the school bake sale and I have not started, so wish me luck.

So the holidays at our house are always a whole production, mostly because my sister-in-law insists on color-coding the gift wrap by recipient, which takes her actual days, and my father-in-law has this tradition of reading a truly terrible poem before anyone's allowed to eat, every single year, and we all have to pretend it's gotten better. This year my brother also brought his new puppy, who spent the entire afternoon trying to steal napkins off people's laps, so there was a lot of chasing involved. For the meal itself, I'd cured the duck legs in salt, thyme, and crushed garlic for a full day, then submerged them in their own rendered fat and let them cook low and slow for hours until the meat practically fell off the bone, crisping the skin under the broiler right before serving alongside a chestnut and prune stuffing. Everyone said it was the best part of the meal, which felt like a win after the poem situation. After dinner we played a ridiculous board game that somehow turned into an actual argument about property values, of all things, and my mother-in-law fell asleep sitting completely upright in her armchair, which is apparently a skill she's had since 1985. We didn't get around to presents until almost ten, by which point the puppy had chewed through at least two bows and one gift tag, and nobody had the energy to be mad about it. Good year overall, though I do think we're retiring the poem next year.

Every year my aunt insists on hosting Diwali at her place, which means every year I spend the drive over bracing myself for the seating chart, because she has never once let two people who dislike each other sit near the food table, and yet somehow it always ends in an argument anyway. This year it was about whether her son's new job counts as a 'real career,' a debate that apparently needed to happen loudly, in the kitchen, next to the rice cooker. The rice itself, for what it's worth, was the one thing nobody argued about — she'd layered basmati that had been soaked and parboiled with whole cardamom pods, cinnamon, and cloves, alternating it with saffron-soaked milk, fried onions gone deep gold, and a spiced meat base, then sealed the pot with a ring of dough pressed around the lid so no steam could escape while it finished cooking over low heat. She always times it so the lid gets cracked open right as people arrive, which is either a happy accident or, knowing her, entirely calculated for maximum effect. After dinner there was the usual round of card games for money that nobody admits is technically gambling, my uncle lost eleven dollars and took it personally, and the porch lights stayed on until well past midnight because someone's kid was terrified of the dark. Same as every year, honestly. I'll be back next year bracing for the seating chart all over again.

You guys, mango sticky rice is just perfect — warm coconut-soaked sticky rice next to cool ripe mango slices, with extra sweetened coconut cream drizzled over the top and a sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds!

Braise 1.2 kg beef short rib at 140°C for three hours in a sauce built from rehydrated guajillo and ancho chiles, blended with garlic, toasted cumin, dried oregano, and a 10 g square of dark chocolate for body. Strain the sauce, reduce by a third, and return the meat to finish. Serve over charred corn tortillas with diced white onion and a lime wedge; internal temperature should read above 90°C for proper collagen breakdown.

We shape the dough by hand into small flower knots, fry until golden, then dip hot into warm honey mixed with orange blossom water and roll in toasted sesame seed — no saffron syrup, just honey and sesame, very fragrant.

Hosting a dinner party is supposed to be relaxing, or so every lifestyle magazine keeps insisting, and yet mine always devolve into some low-grade disaster that I then have to describe at brunch for weeks afterward as 'character building.' This time it was the candles — I bought the wrong size, so every single one either drowned itself in its own wax within twenty minutes or refused to stay upright in the holders, and by the second course half my table looked like a crime scene. My neighbor also showed up an hour early, while I was still in sweatpants arguing with the oven, which set a tone I never fully recovered from. Somewhere in the middle of all that, one dish actually behaved itself: a cold carrot salad, the carrots boiled just until tender then dressed while still warm in olive oil, a good pinch of ground cumin, a spoonful of orange blossom water, and a few slivers of preserved lemon rind stirred through at the end so they didn't turn the whole thing bitter. It sat quietly at the end of the table not causing any trouble whatsoever, unlike everything else that night. By dessert the wax situation had gotten bad enough that someone suggested we just turn off the lights entirely, which honestly improved the ambiance, if not the visibility. Nobody got food poisoning, the important part I suppose, and three people asked for the carrot recipe, which I will absolutely not be sharing because then what would make me special.

ok so we do this stew thing on cold fridays, base is a spicy paste of gochujang and gochugaru mixed with garlic and a splash of the kimchi juice itself, dont skip the juice its the whole point. put it in a wide shallow pot with water and anchovy stock, bring it up slow. chop a block of spam into cubes bc thats whats in the fridge always, throw it in with some ramyeon noodles near the end so they dont turn to mush, and a good handfull of aged kimchi that been sitting a few weeks, sourer the better honestly. baked beans go in too which sounds wierd but trust me. right before it comes off the heat i lay a slice of processed cheese right on top and let it melt into the broth, thats non negotiable in my house, my roommate wont even eat it without the cheese slice now. served straight from the pot in the middle of the table, everyone digs in with their own spoon, no individual bowls, thats half the fun of it. its not a delicate broth like some other stews ppl compare it to, its loud and red and a little chaotic, kinda like the week that led up to friday tbh. leftovers next day are honestly better once the noodles soak up more of the paste.

made the potato thing again last night, slice a big pile of yukon golds real thin on the mandoline, paper thin or it doesnt cook right. rub the baking dish all over with a cut clove of garlic first, dont skip that step it does something. layer the potatoes in slow, each layer gets a little salt, pepper, and fresh grated nutmeg, just a tiny bit or it takes over. then pour warm cream over the whole thing till it just about covers the top layer, i use a mix of cream and a splash of whole milk so it aint too heavy. bake it low, like 300ish, for over an hour covered in foil so the top doesnt burn before the middle sets, then pull the foil off the last 20 min and pile grated gruyere on top so it goes golden and a bit crispy at the edges. the whole house smells like garlic and warm cream by the time its done, which is basically my favorite smell. let it sit 15 min before cutting or it just slides everywhere, learned that the hard way more then once. goes with pretty much any roast, but honestly i could eat a bowl of just this and call it dinner, wich i have done more then i should admit.

At the temple fair each year, my late wife would simmer a fragrant green curry — coconut milk, kaffir lime leaves, galangal, and holy basil folded through eggplant and chicken — ladled generously over jasmine rice for the whole congregation.

My daughter-in-law prepares a small dish of cubed radish, salted then tossed with garlic, ginger, a spoon of fish sauce, and red chili flakes, left to ferment gently on the counter for a day before it graces the table.

I don't even remember when I started making this but the kids request it every single week now, it's just cauliflower and potato cubes tossed in a hot pan with mustard seeds popping first, then turmeric, cumin, and a handful of curry leaves thrown in so fast I always jump a little, and it all cooks down until the potatoes are tender and everything's gone this cheerful yellow color, and honestly some nights it's the only vegetable I can get anyone at this table to eat without a fight, so I'll take it.

Octopus balls are made from a thin batter of flour, dashi, and egg, poured into a half-sphere cast iron pan with deep round molds. Chopped octopus, pickled ginger, and green onion go into each well before the batter sets. Once the edges firm up, a thin skewer or pick is used to rotate each ball a quarter turn, letting raw batter flow into the gap and cook against the hot iron. This turning happens repeatedly, maybe six or seven times per ball, until a fully round crisp shell forms around a soft, almost runny center. Cooked balls are lifted out onto a paper tray, brushed with a thick, slightly sweet brown sauce, then striped with kewpie mayonnaise. Dried bonito flakes are scattered on top last, where the rising heat makes them curl and flutter as if still alive. Powdered dried seaweed sometimes finishes it. Street stalls sell these six or eight to an order, eaten immediately with toothpicks while walking, since the molten center cools fast and the exterior toughens if left sitting. Vendors keep large cast iron pans going continuously, pouring new batter the moment a batch is pulled, cycling dozens of orders an hour during festival crowds. The skill is entirely in the wrist motion for turning; new vendors often end up with lopsided, half-formed shapes before they get the timing down.

Vendors near the gate fry square flatbreads made from layered semolina dough until crisp outside and soft within, then serve them split open with a smear of almond-argan oil paste sweetened with honey.
quick soup tonight, just dashi with a spoon of miso whisked in off heat so it doesnt boil, soft tofu cubes and a scattering of wakame, ready in like 5 min.

Blend 100 g fresh grated coconut with a small piece of ginger, one green chili, and 20 g roasted chana dal, adding water gradually to reach a smooth pourable consistency. Finish with a tempering: heat 15 ml oil, add mustard seeds until they pop, then curry leaves and a pinch of asafoetida, and pour hot over the blended base immediately. Season to taste with salt; store refrigerated up to three days.

The paste starts with a small mountain of dried chilies, shallots, and garlic, all roasted separately in a dry pan until they've gone dark and blistered but not burnt, since bitterness here ruins everything. Once cooled, they're pounded together with a spoonful of dried shrimp, a chunk of fermented shrimp paste, a lump of palm sugar, and a little tamarind pulp until the whole mixture turns into a glossy, almost jammy paste, deep reddish-brown, sweet and smoky and faintly funky all at once. There's no waiting around for this one to ferment on a shelf for months the way some pastes do — it's ready the moment it's pounded smooth, stirred into soups for depth or spread thin over grilled bread as a snack on its own.

Breakfast, steamed not fried:
- rice-and-lentil batter left to ferment overnight
- steamed in small molds till fluffy
- served with coconut chutney, tempered with curry leaves and mustard seed

In my pantry sits a jar of whole lemons, quartered and packed tightly in salt and their own juice for a full month until the rinds turn soft and translucent, ready to be minced into tagines for that particular brightness.

For the new year, the lacquered box gets packed in tiers: vinegared rice topped with strips of raw fish and roe in one layer, simmered black soybeans and sweet chestnut paste in another, thin rolls of kelp tied into knots in a third. Nothing here involves a broth or rice cakes; each item sits dry, arranged deliberately, meant to be eaten cold and slowly over several days, not spooned up hot in one sitting.

For Sunday supper I still prepare my late husband's favorite: lamb shoulder simmered for hours in a conical clay tagine with dried apricots, almonds, cinnamon, and a thread of saffron, until the meat yields to the gentlest touch of a fork.

Okay this dessert is ridiculously easy once you get the hang of it — you dip ladyfingers quickly in strong espresso, just a dunk not a soak, layer them in a dish, then spread a cloud of whipped mascarpone folded with a little sugar and egg yolk over the top, repeat once more, and finish with a generous dusting of cocoa powder right before serving!

So this one time on a trip years ago, I watched a woman at a roadside cart pound green papaya shreds in a big clay mortar with a wooden pestle, tossing in bird's eye chilies, garlic, dried shrimp, a spoon of palm sugar, and a splash of fish sauce, bruising it all together instead of chopping, and she handed me a bag of it with a squeeze of lime and some crushed peanuts on top, and honestly I think about that first bite more than I probably should for something I ate off a folding table on the side of a road.

rolled omelet again this morning, whisk eggs with a splash of dashi and a little sugar, cook thin layers in the rectangle pan and roll each one onto the last till its a fat log, slice and eat with rice.

Combine 60 ml soy sauce, 60 ml rice vinegar, 40 ml fresh yuzu juice, and 10 g kombu, steeped for 24 hours, then strain. A small amount of bonito flakes may be added during steeping for extra depth, strained out before bottling. Store refrigerated; use within two weeks for grilled fish or as a dipping sauce for hot pot.

Every morning I have small espresso, very strong, with warm cornetto filled with apricot jam, standing at the counter of bar near my house, this is normal breakfast for everyone here, very fast, five minutes only.
spent all day making tamales for the party, spread the corn masa thin on soaked husks, spoon in the pork and red chile filling, fold and steam for like an hour till the masa pulls clean off the husk.

Nothing says 'clear your sinuses' quite like a bowl of hot-sour shrimp broth loaded with lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, and enough bird's eye chilies to make you question your life choices by the third spoonful.

I don't make these from scratch, obviously, nobody has time for laminating dough at 7am with three kids yelling about missing shoes, but I do warm the little butter-layered crescents in the oven till they flake apart in your hand, and pair them with the strongest coffee I can manage, and honestly that's breakfast most weekdays, standing at the counter while somebody looks for their other shoe.

Dessert for the party:
- sponge cake soaked in a mix of condensed milk, evaporated milk, and whole milk
- topped with whipped cream
- dusted with cinnamon
- best made a day ahead so it fully absorbs

made a big pot of dal tonight, red lentils boiled soft with turmeric, then i do a tadka on top, ghee, cumin seed, garlic, and dried red chile fried till fragrant and poured sizzling right over the lentils.

Quick side that always disappears fast — morning glory stir-fried hot and hard with garlic, bird's eye chilies, a splash of fish sauce, and a spoon of fermented soybean paste, done in under two minutes so it stays crisp!

For dinner I make paneer cubes in tomato-cashew gravy, tempered first with cumin seed in hot ghee, finish with cream and crushed dry fenugreek leaf on top, very rich, my husband ask for it every week now.

Breakfast this morning was a stack of those spongy semolina pancakes riddled with hundreds of tiny bubbling holes across the surface, made from a thin batter of fine semolina, yeast, and a little flour left to rest until it turns almost foamy, cooked on just one side on a dry, ungreased pan so the top stays soft and porous while the bottom sets golden, then served warm, drizzled generously with a mix of melted butter and honey that pools right down into every single hole.

I have been trying, without much success, to get my houseplants to survive past the two-month mark, and last week I lost yet another pothos to what I can only describe as personal negligence, despite the elaborate watering schedule I built in a spreadsheet that I now suspect I never actually followed. My sister thinks I should just accept that I'm not a plant person and move on to something low-maintenance like rocks, which, fair. Anyway, between mourning the pothos and reorganizing my entire spice cabinet for reasons I still can't fully explain, I did manage to get out to the market street near the station on Saturday, the one lined with carts and plastic stools where the smell of sugar and chili hits you from half a block away. I got a paper tray of the spicy rice cakes, the chewy cylindrical ones simmered down in a thick red sauce built from gochujang, a little sugar, and garlic, with fish cakes and hard-boiled egg halves bobbing around in the same pot, scallions scattered over the top right before it's ladled out. Ate the whole thing standing up at one of those little stools, sauce absolutely everywhere, no regrets. After that I wandered into a bookstore and somehow left with four novels I didn't plan on buying, which is becoming a genuinely worrying pattern at this point, my shelf situation is dire. Still haven't repotted whatever's left of my plant collection. Maybe next weekend, or maybe I finally admit defeat and get the rock.

Holiday bread, made over three days:
- natural yeast starter fed and rested repeatedly before mixing
- enriched dough studded with candied orange peel and raisins
- proofed in a tall paper mold until domed well above the rim
- baked, then hung upside down on skewers to cool so it keeps its structure

Classic sauce, whisked over a bain-marie:
- egg yolks and a shallot-tarragon-vinegar reduction
- clarified butter added slowly, whisking constantly
- finished with more chopped tarragon
- serve warm over grilled steak

Nobody in this family agrees on anything except that New Year's morning means the same bowl every single time: thin ovals of chewy rice cake simmered in a clear beef broth, topped with julienned egg strips and a few threads of dried seaweed, and apparently eating it is the only thing that officially makes you a year older, which feels like a lot of pressure to put on a soup.

A silky vanilla custard, baked slowly in a water bath until just set, chills overnight before a thin layer of sugar is torched on top seconds before serving, hardening into a glassy shell that shatters the instant a spoon breaks through it.

Nothing dignified about eating one of these — a pan-fried sweet dough pocket stuffed with melted brown sugar, cinnamon, and chopped nuts that will absolutely burn your tongue if you don't wait the full sixty seconds everyone always ignores.

ok this side dish is so stupid easy it feels illegal, literally just thick slices of fresh mozzarella stacked with ripe tomato and whole basil leaves, drizzle of good olive oil and a little balsamic on top, flaky salt if you're feeling fancy, zero cooking required and it still looks like you tried.

In my kitchen the mortar and pestle still get regular use, pounding fresh basil leaves with pine nuts, garlic, and a generous measure of grated parmesan until the oil released turns everything a brilliant green — a small ritual I've kept up for decades and refuse to abandon for a food processor.

Today has genuinely been one of those days where I feel like I've been running a small chaotic business with no employees and no days off, starting with the dog somehow getting into the recycling before six am and scattering cereal boxes across the entire kitchen, then a frantic scramble because someone's permission slip was due today and had apparently been sitting crumpled in a backpack since last Tuesday, and then a phone call from the school nurse that turned out to be nothing but still made my stomach drop for a solid ten minutes, and somewhere in the middle of all that I also had to figure out what to do with last night's leftover risotto because I refuse to let it go to waste, so I rolled cold spoonfuls of it around little cubes of mozzarella, pressed them into balls, rolled them in flour then egg then breadcrumbs, and fried them until the outside went deep golden and shattering while the cheese inside turned completely molten, which the kids inhaled in about four minutes flat standing at the counter with paper towels, and then it was back to carpool line, and then a very long conversation with my neighbor about whether her fence is technically on my property line, which I genuinely do not have the bandwidth for this week, and now it's nine pm and I still haven't answered eleven emails, so that's a problem for tomorrow-me, honestly tomorrow-me can handle it.

Two small pancakes, made from a batter leavened with a touch of honey, are cooked on a dry griddle until golden on both sides. Sweetened red bean paste is spread thick between them, then the pair is pressed together into a sandwich. Kept wrapped, the pancakes soften further overnight as moisture from the filling seeps in, which is considered an improvement, not a flaw.

You'll want this dip on everything, I promise — gochujang and doenjang whisked together with sesame oil, a little garlic, and toasted sesame seeds, perfect for wrapping into lettuce with grilled meat!

Ground pork gets stir-fried hard and fast over high heat with garlic, bird's eye chilies, a splash of fish sauce, and a fistful of holy basil tossed in at the very last second so it wilts but keeps its sharp aroma, all piled hot over rice beneath a crispy fried egg.

made the big soup again for iftar, tomatoes blended down with lentils and chickpeas, handfull of cilantro and celery leaf chopped fine, thickened at the end with a flour-water slurry stirred in slow so it doesnt clump, finished with lemon squeezed right into the bowl, always tastes better the next day tbh.

Rice is simmered for over an hour with extra water until it breaks down into a thick, soft porridge. Minced pork is stirred in near the end, along with grated ginger. The bowl is finished with a raw egg cracked on top to cook in the residual heat, crispy fried garlic, chopped scallion, and a dusting of white pepper.

Every Sunday I clear out whatever's wilting in the fridge and turn it into the same soup, kale and cannellini beans simmered down with whatever stale bread ends up torn into it until the whole pot turns thick enough to stand a spoon in, finished with a heavy pour of good olive oil right at the table, and it's somehow better the more days it sits in the fridge, which is the only reason I survive Mondays.
